paras: The attack on Black timber laborers at Donivan (Doniphan), Missouri, took place in late July 1900, when white residents of a town that allowed no Black inhabitants tried to drive out a crew of Black workers brought in by a St. Louis timber company. Several of the workers were roughly handled and some whites and Blacks were injured before the sheriff placed an armed guard around the laborers. Papers outside Missouri reported it as a near "race war," and a Virginia editorial cited it as proof that racial conflict was not confined to the South.

According to a wire dispatch from Poplar Bluff, "No Negroes are allowed to live in the town," and a Missouri weekly opened its item with the statement that "Doniphan has no negro population." The workers were brought in by a St. Louis firm, named in one version of the wire story as the Bagwell Timber company. The Potosi Journal said the company carried the crew to the town in a box car to load 40,000 "crosses" [cross ties].

When the laborers arrived, "the citizens undertook to drive them out," in the words of the wire report. Several of the Black men were "roughly handled," and a number of white men and Black men were hurt, though no report gives a count or names anyone injured. Sheriff Merrill then intervened, and an armed posse took up guard over the workers. The Missouri item described this as a "guard of white men" placed around the laborers to keep down trouble, and it did not mention any violence.

The wire report closed by saying the citizens were determined the workers would not be allowed to remain and that further trouble was expected. No report of arrests, of further clashes, or of whether the crew stayed to finish the work appears in the coverage.

The episode reached readers mainly through a short wire item, printed in Kentucky as "Race War at Donivan, Mo." and in Indiana as "Attack on Negro Laborers." Weekly news digests in Pennsylvania and Minnesota cut it to a single sentence, the Minnesota paper spelling the town "Donovan." These reports repeated the town's exclusion of Black residents as a plain fact and gave the sheriff the role of rescuer, without comment on the residents' demand.

In Missouri the Potosi Journal ran a brief independent item in its state news column, spelling the town Doniphan and giving practical details of the work rather than the language of a race war. The Richmond Times took the case from the New York Herald, which had paired it with the expulsion of Black residents from Spencer County, Indiana, and used both to argue that the race problem was not confined to states south of the Mason and Dixon line. No Black-press coverage of the episode was found.

The town's name differs across reports: the wire printed Donivan, one digest printed Donovan, and the Missouri paper, the source nearest the scene, printed Doniphan. Only the wire report describes beatings and injuries, while the Missouri item speaks only of a guard placed to prevent trouble, without denying that violence occurred.

accounts.label: Wire report (Poplar Bluff, July 29)
accounts.gist: Citizens of Donivan, where no Black people were allowed to live, tried to drive out imported Black laborers; several were roughly handled and whites and Blacks were injured before Sheriff Merrill's armed posse took over guarding them.

accounts.label: Missouri state-news item
accounts.gist: Doniphan has no Black population; a St. Louis timber company brought a crew of colored men in a box car to load ties, and the sheriff placed a guard of white men around them 'to keep down trouble'; no violence is mentioned.

accounts.label: New York Herald, via Richmond Times
accounts.gist: A Missouri sheriff with an armed posse was protecting imported colored laborers from white residents determined that no Black people should live there.

framing.detail: Headlines 'Race War at Donivan, Mo.' and 'Attack on Negro Laborers'; the story says the arrival 'nearly precipitated a race war' and states the town's exclusion of Black residents without comment.
The Potosi Journal gave a short matter-of-fact item opening 'Doniphan has no negro population' and describing the sheriff's guard as keeping down trouble.

The Richmond Times, quoting the New York Herald, used the case together with the Spencer County, Indiana, exodus to argue that the race problem was not confined to the South, in a paragraph defending Southern disfranchisement.

conflicts.note: The Missouri paper (A1) is the nearest source and its item matches the wire story in employer, laborers and sheriff's guard; Donivan and Donovan are likely wire misspellings, but no source says so.
